subtype: Approach: freelance income as a bridge [Action]
passage: People think a real founder lives on noodles and hope. I tried that for two months. I'm Avni, by the way. What actually saved the company was taking two part-time programming contracts, ten hours a week each, that paid my rent and food. That meant every rupee in the startup account went to the product: the designer, the servers, the testing. It felt like a step backwards at first, like admitting the startup wasn't enough. But it bought us about five more months of runway. Bhavna, my co-founder, said it best: "You're not leaving the startup. You're refuelling it." I still write code for other people on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the product is better for the time it got.

qa.a: Avni took two part-time programming contracts.

qa.q: How did Avni feel at first about taking the contracts?
qa.a: Avni felt uneasy about it, since it seemed like a step backwards and like admitting the startup wasn't enough.

qa.q: What should Avni watch out for while doing this?
qa.a: Avni should keep the contract hours fixed so that the outside work does not eat the time the product needs.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see Avni's decision?
qa.a: Bhavna seems supportive, describing it as refuelling the startup rather than leaving it.

grounding: Avni takes two part-time contracts to cover personal rent and food so the startup money goes to product and lasts about five months longer.

subtype: Approach: freelance income as a bridge [Action]
passage:
Tejas and I share a flat in Pune and a startup, so I saw the whole thing up close. In March our company account had seven months left. Tejas came home one night and said, "I've taken two consulting contracts. Mornings only, backend work for a logistics firm and a school."
I was annoyed at first; I thought he was losing faith in our product. But he had done the maths on the fridge whiteboard. If his rent and food came from consulting, the company money only had to pay for servers and my stipend. He crossed out "seven months" and wrote "twelve".
From then on he consulted till noon, ate lunch standing up and switched to our app. He looked tired some weeks. But in September, when other founders we knew were shutting down, we still had money in the bank.
— Uday

What might Tejas have been feeling some weeks, from what Uday saw?
qa.a: Tejas may have felt tired and stretched, though he kept going; Uday can only see the tired look.

qa.q: What else could protect the product work while Tejas consults?
qa.a: They could keep fixed afternoon hours for the app and check each month whether the consulting is squeezing the product.

qa.q: How did Uday's view of the contracts change?
qa.a: Uday was annoyed at first, thinking Tejas had lost faith, but came to see the contracts as buying five more months.

grounding: It shows a founder taking two part-time consulting contracts to cover his own rent and food, so company money goes to the product and the runway grows by five months.

subtype: Approach: freelance income as a bridge [Action]
passage:
Monday, 6 January. Yogesh and Kavitha stare at the spreadsheet in their Hyderabad office-cum-bedroom. Company money left: eight months, much of it going on Yogesh's rent and groceries. "We'll run out before the product is ready," Kavitha says.
Thursday, 16 January. Yogesh signs two part-time contracts: one maintaining a hospital billing system, one training interns at a software firm, twenty hours a week in total. The pay covers his rent and food. He stops drawing money from the company.
Friday, 30 May. Kavitha updates the sheet. Because the company now pays only for product costs, the runway reads thirteen months. Yogesh is tired on Tuesdays, when both contracts overlap, but the first paying clinic has just signed.

qa.q: How many hours a week were the two contracts in total?
qa.a: Twenty hours a week in total.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she said "We'll run out before the product is ready"?
qa.a: Kavitha was anxious and discouraged about how little runway was left.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do about the tiring Tuesdays?
qa.a: He could ask one client to move hours so the contracts don't overlap, protecting his energy for product work.

qa.q: How does the change look to Kavitha by May?
qa.a: Kavitha sees the runway stretched to thirteen months and a first paying clinic signed, so the plan clearly paid off.

grounding: It shows a founder taking part-time contracts to pay personal rent and food, freeing company money for product work and extending the runway by five months.
